candidate.answerReason: For each possible first-pass endpoint k, there are C(13,k)-1 valid arrangements. Summing over 1≤k≤12 gives 2^13-2-12=8178.

methods.label: Method 1: Choose positions for the two passes
methods.explanation:
Each pass picks up a consecutive group of card numbers. Suppose the first pass ends with card \(k\), where \(1\leq k\leq12\). Then cards \(1,\ldots,k\) must appear from left to right in increasing order, and so must cards \(k+1,\ldots,13\).

Choose the \(k\) positions occupied by the first group. Fill those positions with \(1,\ldots,k\) in order, and fill the remaining positions with \(k+1,\ldots,13\) in order. Thus there are \(\binom{13}{k}\) arrangements with these two internal orders.

For the first pass to stop at \(k\), card \(k+1\) must lie to the left of card \(k\). If instead \(k\) lies before \(k+1\), both internal orders force the entire row to be \(1,2,\ldots,13\). This is the only arrangement to exclude. Every other arrangement constructed this way takes exactly two passes: the first collects through \(k\), and the second collects the remaining increasing group.

Every valid arrangement has a unique first-pass endpoint, so the cases neither overlap nor omit any valid row. The required count is therefore
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{12}\left(\binom{13}{k}-1\right).
\]
The sum of \(\binom{13}{k}\) over all \(k=0,\ldots,13\) is \(2^{13}\), because each of the 13 positions can independently be chosen or not chosen. Removing the empty and full selections, then the one excluded arrangement in each of the 12 cases, gives
\[
2^{13}-2-12=8192-14=8178.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{8178}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses elementary position choices, disjoint cases, and a binomial sum justified by independent choices.

methods.label: Method 2: Count by inserting the largest entry
methods.explanation:
Let \(p_i\) be the original position of card \(i\), counting positions from the left. After collecting card \(i\), we can collect card \(i+1\) on the same pass exactly when \(p_i<p_{i+1}\). If \(p_i>p_{i+1}\), a new pass is needed. Call such a decrease between consecutive entries a descent. Exactly two passes therefore means exactly one descent in the list \(p_1,\ldots,p_{13}\).

This position list is itself a permutation of \(1,\ldots,13\). Conversely, any such list uniquely specifies the card arrangement by placing card \(i\) in position \(p_i\). Thus we can count permutations with exactly one descent.

Let \(a_n\) be the number of permutations of \(1,\ldots,n\) with exactly one descent. Build these by inserting \(n\) into a permutation of \(1,\ldots,n-1\). Inserting \(n\) at the end adds no descent; inserting it at the beginning adds one. Between entries \(u,v\), it replaces their comparison with \(u<n>v\), which has exactly one descent. In particular, insertion never decreases the number of descents.

There are consequently two possible starting types:

If the shorter permutation has one descent, inserting \(n\) at that descent or at the end preserves exactly one descent. This gives \(2a_{n-1}\) possibilities.

If the shorter permutation has no descent, it is the unique increasing permutation. Any insertion except at the end produces one descent, giving \(n-1\) possibilities.

These cases are exhaustive, and deleting \(n\) uniquely recovers the shorter permutation and insertion place, so nothing is counted twice. Hence, for \(n\geq2\),
\[
a_n=2a_{n-1}+n-1,\qquad a_1=0.
\]
To simplify this recurrence, set \(b_n=a_n+n+1\). Then
\[
b_n=2(a_{n-1}+n)=2b_{n-1},
\]
and \(b_1=2\). Repeated doubling gives \(b_n=2^n\), so
\[
a_{13}=2^{13}-13-1=8178.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{8178}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
